analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to sell to states and localities at the lower prices they charge abroad.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House committee until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: States and local governments pay some of the highest drug prices in the world for their employees, retirees, and Medicaid beneficiaries. This bill would have required any drug maker that contracts with the federal government to also sell to states and localities at prices no higher than the maker's average price in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom. The bill's findings estimated this could cut brand-name drug prices for states by up to 40 percent. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee, where it died without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local government employees, retirees, and Medicaid and pharmaceutical-assistance beneficiaries would get prescription drugs at prices comparable to those in other wealthy countries. State and local budgets would benefit directly: the bill's findings cite healthcare spending at roughly 30 percent of state budgets and Medicaid cost growth in the double digits, and estimated price reductions of up to 40 percent on brand-name drugs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: State employees, retirees, and Medicaid patients

how_it_helps.text: Each drug manufacturer that contracts with the federal government would have to make drugs available to states and local governments, for their group health, retiree, and pharmaceutical assistance programs (including Medicaid), at a price no greater than the manufacturer's average foreign price in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, or the United Kingdom.

The bill states its purpose is 'substantial reductions' in drug prices for state and local government programs, and its findings estimate the policy could reduce prices for brand-name drugs for many states and localities by up to 40 percent.

Enforcement would be strong: the government, wholesalers, retailers, and affected residents could sue, and courts could award three times the overcharge; manufacturers with repeated violations could be barred from federal contracting.
States could choose either to keep their Medicaid rebate agreements or to buy at foreign prices instead, and states remain free to pursue programs with even lower prices.

The bill responds to a documented fiscal squeeze: its findings cite state healthcare cost growth of 11 percent in 2002, Medicaid cost growth of 13 percent in fiscal 2002, and 37 states cutting fiscal 2003 budgets by nearly $14.5 billion.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost, accepting lower effective prices on drugs sold to state and local programs — bringing those U.S. prices closer to what they already accept in other developed countries — and facing treble damages and possible federal debarment for violations.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: capping U.S. prices at foreign averages would cut manufacturer revenue on a large share of U.S. drug sales, which pharmaceutical makers argue could reduce investment in developing new drugs. The bill contains no answer to that concern beyond a study of whether prices were reduced.

The foreign-price benchmark is complex to compute — it must account for rebates, side agreements, bundling arrangements, and dosage differences across six countries — leaving substantial room for regulatory disputes and litigation over what the true 'average foreign price' is.
The bill does not directly lower prices for people buying insurance privately or paying cash at the pharmacy; its benefits flow only through state and local government drug programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to taxpayers and state-program beneficiaries is large and concrete — state drug spending was consuming roughly 30 percent of state budgets and growing faster than revenue, and the bill targeted price cuts of up to 40 percent on brand-name drugs. The main cost falls on an industry that already sells the same drugs profitably at lower prices in every covered foreign country. The genuine trade-off is the possible long-run effect on drug-company research spending, which the bill acknowledges only by requiring reports to Congress. On balance the design is straightforward: tie U.S. prices for government purchasers to prices the same companies already accept abroad, with real enforcement teeth.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee on December 8 and 17, 2003, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Allen of Maine introduced the bill on December 8, 2003, joined as original cosponsors by 16 other House members including Henry Waxman, Sherrod Brown, and one Republican, Jo Ann Emerson.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced.
Nine days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it remained for the rest of the Congress.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because they continued selling to state and local government programs at full U.S. prices instead of the lower prices the bill would have required. State budgets and their prescription drug beneficiaries gained nothing, and remain exposed to the price growth the bill cited.

for.name: Rep. Thomas H. Allen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan set of original cosponsors.

for.name: 17 House cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Henry Waxman, Sherrod Brown, Frank Pallone, Ed Markey, and John Dingall-aligned Democrats plus one Republican, Jo Ann Emerson
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; one of the 18 cosponsors was a Republican.

for.name: National Governors Association
for.what_they_did: Passed a resolution in February 2002 urging Congress to review federal laws contributing to the high cost of prescription drugs, which the bill cites as a finding.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Billy Tauzin (R-LA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it was referred to committee on December 8, 2003, then to the Health subcommittee, and no action followed for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Industry whose U.S. prices the bill would cap at foreign levels
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial interest in the bill's defeat; the bill would impose price caps and treble-damages liability on any manufacturer contracting with the federal government.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had 18 cosponsors — 17 Democrats and just 1 Republican (Jo Ann Emerson) — and died in a committee controlled by the House Republican majority without ever reaching the floor, so support was overwhelmingly from one party while the chamber was controlled by the other.

industries.note: The bill would cap the prices these companies could charge state and local government drug programs at their average foreign price across six developed countries — roughly the prices they already accept elsewhere — with treble-damages lawsuits and federal debarment for repeat violations. Their continued ability to charge U.S. government purchasers far more than foreign ones was preserved when the bill died.

State program purchases would continue to flow through pharmacies, and the bill explicitly allows a Secretary-approved reasonable handling fee. Cheaper drugs could also increase demand through state programs.

The bill gives wholesalers and retailers, alongside the government and affected residents, standing to sue manufacturers for treble damages when drugs are sold above the foreign-price benchmark — a new enforcement tool in their favor.
